title: RC High-Pass Filter: Why Gain Rolls In Past the Cutoff
topic: RC high-pass filter — swap the roles of R and C: capacitor in series, resistor to ground; H(jω) = jωRC / (1 + jωRC); gain rises at +20 dB/decade below the cutoff ω_c = 1/RC and is flat (0 dB) above; phase shifts from +90° down to 0°

beats.narration: Swap the R and the C in our filter — what changes?

elements.content: Manimo bobs in centre-screen
Same parts, swapped positions — which way does the gain go?

beats.narration: The capacitor sits in series; the resistor goes to ground; V out is taken across the resistor.

elements.content: V_in terminal pair on the left, top wire to capacitor plates in series
Capacitor (two amber plates) in series on the top wire
Resistor R from the V_out node down to ground rail
C label above the capacitor, R label beside the resistor
V_out terminal pair on the right
H(jω) = jωRC / (1 + jωRC)
elements.position: below the diagram, large serif italic

beats.narration: Step the input frequency from low to high. At low frequencies the capacitor blocks the signal and V out collapses. As the frequency climbs past the cutoff, V out grows up to match V in.

elements.content: Two stacked panels — V_in (top, constant amplitude) and V_out (bottom, amplitude grows with frequency)
V_in sinusoid drawn at unit amplitude every frame
V_out sinusoid amplitude = x/√(1+x²), phase lead = π/2 − atan(x)
Live ω/ω_c readout and |H| readout below the panels

beats.narration: Plot the gain in decibels against frequency on a log axis. Below the cutoff the gain climbs at twenty decibels every decade; above the cutoff it is flat at zero dB.

elements.content: Bode magnitude plot with log ω/ω_c on x-axis (4 decades) and dB on y-axis (−45 to +5)
Dashed vertical at ω_c with rose marker
Asymptotes: +20 dB/dec for x < 1, flat at 0 dB for x > 1
Full magnitude curve revealed left to right by a sweeping cursor
+20 dB/decade slope annotation in the low-frequency region

beats.narration: Above omega equals one over R C the filter passes the signal through. Below, it kills low frequencies — that is why we call it a high pass filter.

elements.content: ω_c = 1 / RC
elements.position: centre, large amber serif italic — same cutoff formula as the low-pass

elements.content: high frequencies pass through; low frequencies are attenuated
the same shape drives DC blockers, AC coupling, edge detectors
